abstract: This paper presents a task-based framework for modeling the economic consequences of AI capabilities growth between 2026 and 2030. The model maps AI automation of cognitive work into paths for GDP, labor share, wages, and unemployment across three scenarios. Under modest change, AI adds less than half a point to GDP growth; under extreme change, AI performs nearly half of today's cognitive work, GDP grows to 15 percent annually, the labor share falls from 60 to 45 percent, and cognitive worker unemployment reaches nearly 20 percent. A survey of 10,980 US adults indicates public expectations align closest with the substantial change scenario.
keyFindings: Under the extreme scenario by 2030, AI automation raises GDP 32.4 percent above the no-AI path with 15.4 percent annual growth, while the labor share falls from 60 to 45 percent of income.

Cognitive occupations experience divergent outcomes across scenarios: wages decline 11.5 percent in the extreme scenario while unemployment among cognitive workers reaches 17.9 percent, versus 2.9 percent in the no-AI baseline.

In the extreme scenario, total labor income remains nearly unchanged while all GDP gains accrue to capital income (81 percent above baseline), requiring transfers of approximately 9 percent of GDP to maintain cognitive workers' income.

Public survey expectations (median n=3,259) center on outcomes consistent with the substantial scenario: GDP 8.6 percent above baseline, cognitive employment decline of 4.2 percent, and cognitive unemployment of 4.6 percent.

The model shows wage rigidity critically determines labor market adjustment: at full wage flexibility cognitive wages fall 42.2 percent with 2.6 percent unemployment; at high rigidity cognitive wages rise 2.8 percent but unemployment reaches 24.0 percent.
methodology: Task-based computational model calibrated to mid-2026 baseline using CPS employment data (cognitive occupations comprise 62.4 percent of employment) and Census BTOS data on AI adoption (18 percent of firms, 32 percent employment-weighted in late 2025). Three scenarios parameterized by five AI-related objects (task mass, diffusion, productivity gain, automation share, reinstatement ratio) and two labor-market frictions (search discount, posting speed). Survey component: 10,980 US adults surveyed via Morning Consult August 11-23, 2026, on five items regarding AI capability timelines, task coverage, speed gains, augmentation versus automation, and job search duration. Respondent parameters (n=3,259 completing all items) run through the model to generate predicted outcomes with interquartile ranges.
qualifiers: The scenarios are not predictions and no probabilities are attached. The framework omits catastrophic risks, political economy, business cycles, financial market disruptions, price rigidities and associated demand effects, AI in household production, and data-center buildout effects. Worker heterogeneity is very coarse—workers differ only by employment status and occupation group, with displaced workers earning the destination wage immediately with no tenure discount. The model does not follow individual workers and considers only cognitive tasks, excluding rapid robotics advances, which is why analysis stops at 2030. External reviewers (including Acemoglu, Autor, Moll, Nakamura, Restrepo, Romer, Steinsson) were not asked to endorse conclusions. Some reviewers questioned whether exposed occupations will shrink at all, whether the extreme scenario is overstated as a thought experiment, and whether the modest scenario understates current observable trends.
